name: ls
whatItDoes: Prints the names of files and directories. With flags it also shows sizes, owners, permissions and timestamps.
arguments: files or directories to list (default: the current directory)
options: include hidden entries (names starting with a dot)
long format: permissions, owner, size, modified time
human-readable sizes such as 4.0K or 1.2M (use with -l)
sort by modification time, newest first
list a directory itself instead of its contents
examples: long listing of your home directory including hidden files
newest files last: handy at the end of a long listing
only the directories in the current folder

name: cd
whatItDoes: A shell built-in that moves your shell into another directory. Without an argument it goes to your home directory.
arguments: where to go; relative to the current directory unless it starts with /
options: go to your home directory (same as plain cd)
go to another user's home directory
examples: toggle back to where you just were
notes: cd is built into the shell, so it has no man page of its own; use help cd in bash.

name: pwd
whatItDoes: Shows the full path of the directory your shell is in.
options: show the logical path, keeping symbolic links as you typed them (default)
show the physical path with symbolic links resolved
examples: the real location when you are inside a symlinked directory

name: cp
whatItDoes: Copies one or more files to a destination. Existing destination files are overwritten without asking unless you use -i.
arguments: target file, or an existing directory to copy into
options: print each file as it is copied
archive: recursive and preserve attributes (GNU and recent macOS)
notes: Without -i or -n, cp silently replaces an existing destination file.

name: mv
whatItDoes: Moves files to another place or renames them. Within one filesystem it is instant and keeps the data in place.
arguments: new name, or a directory to move into
examples: move many files into a directory
notes: mv silently overwrites an existing destination unless you use -i or -n.

name: rm
whatItDoes: Deletes files permanently. There is no trash can and no undo, so check the path before you press Enter.
options: remove directories and everything inside them
never prompt and ignore missing files
examples: delete temp files, confirming each one
delete a directory and its contents
delete a file whose name starts with a dash
notes: rm -rf with a wrong path or an unquoted variable is how data gets lost. Prefer rm -i while learning, and put -- before names that begin with a dash.

name: ln
whatItDoes: Makes a second name for a file. A hard link shares the same data; a symbolic link (-s) is a small file that points to a path.
options: create a symbolic link instead of a hard link
examples: put a tool on your PATH with a symlink
make a hard link to a file
notes: Hard links cannot cross filesystems or point to directories; symbolic links can do both and can dangle if the target is removed.

name: mkdir
whatItDoes: Creates one or more empty directories.
arguments: name of the directory to create
options: create missing parent directories and do not fail if it already exists
set the permission mode, for example -m 700
examples: create a whole path at once

name: touch
explanation: create an empty file or update timestamps
whatItDoes: Creates the file if it does not exist, otherwise just updates its access and modification times.
examples: update the time only if the file exists

name: cat
whatItDoes: Writes the contents of files to the terminal, in order. With no file it copies standard input.
arguments: files to print, joined in the order given
options: squeeze repeated blank lines into one
examples: join two files into a third
show a file with line numbers
notes: For long files use less. Redirecting onto a file you are reading from (cat f > f) empties it.

name: less
whatItDoes: Shows a file one screen at a time without loading it all, with searching and scrolling.
arguments: file to view (or pipe text into less)
options: case-insensitive search unless the pattern has capitals
examples: page the output of another command
read a file with line numbers
notes: Keys inside less: space = next page, b = back, /text = search, n = next match, G = end, g = start, q = quit.

name: head
explanation: show the start of a file
whatItDoes: Prints the first lines (10 by default) of each file.
options: number of lines to show, for example -n 20
number of bytes to show instead of lines
examples: the first five entries of a listing

name: tail
explanation: show the end of a file
whatItDoes: Prints the last lines (10 by default); with -f it keeps watching the file for new lines.
options: follow: keep printing lines as they are appended
follow and keep trying if the file is rotated or recreated
examples: watch a log live (Ctrl+C to stop)

name: file
explanation: identify a file by its content
whatItDoes: Looks at the bytes of a file, not its name, and says what it appears to be.
options: brief: omit the file name from the output
print only the MIME type, such as text/plain
examples: what kind of file is this?
notes: Useful for forensics and CTF work where extensions lie.

name: find
explanation: search for files by name, type, size or time
whatItDoes: Walks a directory tree and prints the files that match your conditions. It can also run a command on each match.
arguments: where to start searching (default: the current directory)
options: match the file name against a pattern; quote it: -name "*.log"
f for files, d for directories, l for symlinks
modified N days ago; -mtime -1 means within the last day
size test such as +10M (larger than 10 MiB)
match permissions, for example -perm -4000 for setuid
do not descend more than N levels (put it before the tests)
run a command on each match: -exec cmd {} \;
examples: list setuid programs, hiding permission errors
directories at most two levels down
notes: -delete and -exec act on everything matched. Run the search without them first and read the list.

name: du
explanation: show disk usage of files and directories
whatItDoes: Reports how much space files and directory trees use.
arguments: files or directories to measure (default: the current directory)
options: show only a total for each argument
examples: size of everything in this folder
how big is my Downloads folder?
the ten largest items below here
notes: To limit depth use --max-depth=N on GNU/Linux or -d N on macOS.

name: df
whatItDoes: Reports total, used and free space for each mounted filesystem.
arguments: show only the filesystem that holds this path
options: show inode usage instead of blocks
examples: free space on every mounted disk
check whether you have run out of inodes
notes: A disk can be "full" because it ran out of inodes even when space remains; check df -i.

name: tar
whatItDoes: Bundles many files into one archive and unpacks them again, optionally compressing with gzip, bzip2 or xz.
arguments: the .tar / .tar.gz file to create or read
options: the archive file name (must come right before it)
change to this directory before extracting
notes: Extracting overwrites files with the same name. List an unknown archive with -t first.

name: grep
whatItDoes: Prints lines that match a pattern, from files or from standard input.
arguments: text or regular expression to look for
files to search (omit to read standard input)
options: invert: show lines that do not match
list only the names of files that match
show N lines of context around each match, for example -C 2
examples: find TODO comments with file and line number
ps aux | grep -v grep | grep ssh
lines starting with root: or admin:

name: sed
whatItDoes: Applies editing commands to each line, most often a substitution like s/old/new/.
arguments: files to process (omit to read standard input)
options: print only lines selected with the p command
add a script; can be repeated
edit the file in place (GNU: -i; macOS needs -i "")
examples: replace every foo with bar and print the result
edit in place, keeping a .bak copy
notes: -i rewrites the file. Use -i.bak to keep a backup until you are sure.

name: awk
whatItDoes: Splits each line into fields ($1, $2, …) and runs a small program on them. Great for columns and quick sums.
arguments: pattern { action } pairs, in single quotes
files to read (omit for standard input)
options: set the field separator, for example -F: or -F,
set a variable before running: -v name=value
examples: print the first column of every line
lines where the third field is above 100
notes: Built-ins: NR is the line number, NF the number of fields, $0 the whole line.

name: sort
whatItDoes: Sorts lines alphabetically by default; flags change the order and the key.
arguments: files to sort (omit for standard input)
options: keep only the first of equal lines
sort by a field: -k2 sorts on the second field
sort human-readable sizes such as 2K and 1G
examples: sort a CSV by its second column

name: uniq
whatItDoes: Removes or counts adjacent duplicate lines, so the input normally needs to be sorted first.
arguments: file to read (omit for standard input)
options: prefix each line with how many times it occurred
show only lines that were repeated
show only lines that were not repeated
examples: rank values by how often they appear
which words appear more than once?

name: cut
whatItDoes: Prints selected fields or characters from each line.
arguments: files to read (omit for standard input)
options: which fields to print, such as -f1 or -f1,3
which character positions to print, such as -c1-8
examples: take the year from a date
notes: cut cannot handle quoted CSV fields that contain the delimiter; use awk or a CSV tool for that.

name: wc
whatItDoes: Counts how much text a file or a stream contains.
arguments: files to count (omit for standard input)
examples: how many entries in this folder?

name: tr
whatItDoes: Reads standard input and swaps, squeezes or deletes characters. It does not take file names.
notes: tr works on single characters, not words: tr "ab" "xy" maps a→x and b→y.

name: diff
whatItDoes: Shows what changed between two files or two directories.
options: unified format, the one patches and code review use
examples: which files differ between two folders?
notes: Lines starting with - exist only in the first file, lines starting with + only in the second.

name: xargs
whatItDoes: Turns lines or words from a pipe into arguments for another command.
arguments: the command to run with the collected arguments (default: echo)
options: use at most N arguments per run
replace a placeholder such as {} with each input item
items are separated by NUL bytes (pair with find -print0)
run up to N commands in parallel
print each command before running it
examples: files containing a word, safe for odd names
copy each match, using {} as the placeholder
notes: Preview with -t or echo before using xargs with rm or mv.

name: chmod
whatItDoes: Sets who may read, write or execute a file or directory.
options: symbolic: give the owner read and write
examples: private key readable only by you
owner full, others read and enter
notes: Numeric modes: r=4, w=2, x=1, summed per owner / group / others. chmod -R 777 is almost never the answer.

name: chown
whatItDoes: Changes who owns a file. Usually needs root.
arguments: new owner, optionally followed by a group
options: change a symlink itself, not its target
examples: set owner and group for a web root
notes: chown -R on the wrong directory (for example /) can break a system. Double-check the path.

name: sudo
explanation: run a command with another user's privileges
whatItDoes: Runs one command as root (or another user) after checking /etc/sudoers.
arguments: the command to run with elevated privileges
options: run as this user instead of root
list the commands you are allowed to run
start a login shell as the target user
examples: run a package command as root
what may I run with sudo?
run a command as the postgres user
notes: sudo -l is a first step in privilege-escalation checks. Prefer one sudo command over a long root shell (least privilege).

name: id
whatItDoes: Prints the numeric and named user ID, primary group and all groups of a user.
options: print only the primary group ID
print names instead of numbers (with -u, -g or -G)
examples: who am I and which groups am I in?

name: ping
whatItDoes: Sends ICMP echo requests and reports whether and how fast replies come back.
arguments: name or IP address to test
options: stop after N packets (otherwise it runs until Ctrl+C)
size of the packet payload in bytes
notes: On Windows the count flag is -n. A firewall that drops ICMP makes a healthy host look dead.

name: curl
explanation: transfer data from or to a URL
whatItDoes: Makes HTTP(S) and other requests from the command line. The standard tool for poking at web APIs.
options: save output to a file name you choose
save using the remote file name
choose the HTTP method, for example -X POST
send data in the request body
verbose: show the request and response headers
examples: inspect the TLS and header exchange
notes: -k disables the protection TLS gives you; use it only against your own lab hosts.

name: dig
whatItDoes: Asks a DNS server for records and shows the full answer, including TTLs and flags.
arguments: record type such as A, AAAA, MX, TXT, NS (default A)
options: ask a specific DNS server, for example @1.1.1.1
reverse lookup of an IP address
follow delegation from the root servers down
examples: full answer for the A record
TXT records from a chosen resolver
which name does this IP have?

name: ssh
explanation: log in to a remote machine securely
whatItDoes: Opens an encrypted shell (or runs one command) on another machine, and can tunnel network traffic.
arguments: account and machine to connect to
optional command to run instead of a shell
options: dynamic SOCKS proxy on a local port
do not run a command (for tunnels only)
examples: reach the remote web server at http://localhost:8080
reach an internal host through a jump box
notes: Verify the host key fingerprint on first connect, and keep private keys at chmod 600.

name: scp
whatItDoes: Copies files between machines using ssh for transport and authentication.
examples: upload a folder over a custom port
notes: Like cp, scp overwrites existing destination files without asking.

name: nmap
whatItDoes: Discovers hosts and open ports and can identify services and versions. Only scan systems you own or have written permission to test.
arguments: host name, IP address or network range (for example 192.0.2.0/24)
options: ping scan: find live hosts without scanning ports
ports to scan, such as -p 22,80 or -p-
skip host discovery and assume the host is up
aggressive: version, OS, scripts and traceroute
save normal output to a file
examples: service versions on three common ports
which hosts are up on this network?
scan the project's own permitted test host
notes: Scanning machines you do not have permission for can be illegal. scanme.nmap.org is provided for light testing; your own lab VMs are better.

name: ss
whatItDoes: Lists open sockets and listening ports. The modern replacement for netstat on Linux.
options: show numbers instead of resolving names
show the owning process (needs root for other users)
examples: every listening TCP/UDP port and its process
notes: On macOS use netstat -an or lsof -i instead.

name: tcpdump
whatItDoes: Prints packets crossing a network interface, optionally filtered, or saves them for Wireshark. Needs root.
arguments: a capture filter such as port 53 or host 192.0.2.10
options: interface to listen on (any listens on all)
do not resolve names; -nn also skips port names
write raw packets to a file
more detail; repeat for even more
examples: twenty packets to or from one host
save a capture for later analysis
notes: Capture only on networks you are authorised to monitor; captures can contain passwords and personal data.

name: nc
whatItDoes: Netcat opens TCP/UDP connections or listens on a port, which makes it handy for testing services and moving small amounts of data.
options: scan: connect and close without sending data
examples: which of ports 20 to 25 are open?
wait for one connection on port 4444 (OpenBSD/macOS nc)
send one line to a listener
notes: Netcat versions differ: traditional (GNU) nc needs -p to set a listen port (nc -l -p 4444).

name: ip
explanation: show and manage network interfaces and routes
whatItDoes: The modern Linux tool for addresses, links and routing (replaces ifconfig and route).
examples: interfaces and their addresses at a glance
show the routing table and default gateway
notes: On macOS use ifconfig and netstat -rn.

name: man
explanation: read the manual page for a command
whatItDoes: Opens the reference manual for a command, file format or library function.
arguments: optional section number, such as 5 for file formats
options: search page names and descriptions for a keyword (apropos)
show a one-line description of a page (whatis)
examples: the format of /etc/passwd, not the passwd command
notes: Inside man: space = next page, / = search, n = next match, q = quit. Built-ins like cd are documented in help.

name: ps
whatItDoes: Takes a snapshot of the processes running on the machine.
options: BSD style: every process with its user, CPU and memory
UNIX style: every process with parent PIDs
notes: ps aux | grep name also matches the grep itself; use pgrep name for a cleaner search.

name: kill
explanation: send a signal to a process
whatItDoes: Asks a process to stop (SIGTERM by default) or sends it another signal. Despite the name it does not always kill.
arguments: process ID(s) from ps or pgrep
options: SIGKILL: stop immediately; the process cannot clean up
hang up: many daemons reload their config
examples: force it to stop if it ignores the polite request
tell a daemon to reload its configuration
notes: Try plain kill first; -9 skips cleanup and can leave locks or half-written files. Use pkill name or killall name to match by name.
